articles.title: In 2003, Sean and Melodye Rooney bought Montana land beside the Stillwater River; 23 years later, their 57-acre property with nearly a mile of river frontage became permanently protected from development
articles.summary: A piece of Montana land that the Rooney family has called home for more than two decades will remain undeveloped for generations to come.
articles.body: A piece of Montana land that the Rooney family has called home for more than two decades will remain undeveloped for generations to come. Sean and Melodye Rooney have placed a conservation easement on their 57-acre property west of Whitefish, permanently preventing subdivision and development across the land. According to the Flathead Beacon, the family worked with the Flathead Land Trust to protect nearly a mile of Stillwater River frontage. The property includes wetlands, riparian forest and more than 20 acres of hay ground, while its location alongside other protected and public lands makes it part of a larger stretch of conserved habitat.A family connection to the landThe Rooneys' relationship with the Flathead Valley goes back well before they purchased the Stillwater River property. Sean Rooney's grandfather homesteaded near Cut Bank before eventually working for the Great Northern Railway in Whitefish. His father later returned to the Flathead Valley after years of travelling internationally and taught English and geology at Flathead Valley Community College. Sean and Melodye bought the property with Sean's parents in 2003. They eventually became the sole owners and now live there year-round.Over the years, the land became more than simply a place for the family to live. They spent time observing the wildlife that moved through the property and working to maintain its natural features. That connection helped shape the decision to place the land under a conservation easement.Nearly a mile of river frontage will stay intactThe 57-acre property contains nearly a mile of frontage along the Stillwater River. Its landscape includes riparian forest, shrubland and wetlands, alongside more than 20 acres of land that remains in hay production. Those different habitats make the property useful to a wide range of species. Camera traps on the land have recorded grizzly and black bears, mountain lions, gray wolves, moose, river otters and bald eagles. The property's importance also extends beyond the animals that pass through it. Its river frontage and wetlands help support the health of the Stillwater River, which provides habitat for bull trout and westslope cutthroat trout.In 2025, the family began a habitat enhancement project focused on restoring a ponded area and the wetland habitat around it, adding another layer to their efforts to maintain the property's ecological value.Wildlife has been documented on the propertyThe Rooneys have been able to see just how much wildlife uses the land through their involvement in Snapshot USA, a nationwide mammal survey coordinated annually by the Smithsonian Institution. The property serves as an official study site for the programme, with camera traps recording animals moving through the area. One particularly striking example came when the family's daughter, Brigit Rooney, checked a camera memory card and found a photograph of herself walking along the property. Only eight minutes later, the same trail was captured with a mountain lion passing through.For Flathead Land Trust, the wildlife value of the property was apparent from its first visit. The organisation's Ryan Hunter saw a bear swimming across the Stillwater River below the family's house. These observations helped reinforce the importance of keeping the property intact as part of the river corridor.What the conservation easement changesThe agreement with Flathead Land Trust does not mean the Rooneys have given up ownership of their property. Instead, the conservation easement permanently limits what can happen to the land in the future. Subdivision and development are barred, while the family can continue to own and manage the property. That distinction is important because the land can remain a working property while its natural features are protected. Hay production can continue, and the family can continue living on and caring for the land.Flathead Land Trust describes conservation easements as voluntary legal agreements that allow landowners to retain ownership while protecting wildlife habitat, wetlands, riparian areas and open space in perpetuity. The organisation monitors properties under its easements and is responsible for ensuring that the terms of each agreement are followed.One more piece of a larger protected corridorThe Rooney property also sits in an unusually connected setting. It borders two existing Flathead Land Trust conservation easements and is near land managed by the U.S. Forest Service and Stillwater State Forest. Protecting the 57 acres therefore adds another privately owned piece to an already connected landscape of conserved and public land. Flathead Land Trust said the new easement strengthens an interconnected corridor along the Stillwater River and Highway 93, helping keep both wildlife habitat and agricultural land intact.For the Rooneys, the decision means the land they purchased in 2003 will not eventually be divided into smaller properties or replaced by development. Instead, the river frontage, wetlands, hay fields and wildlife habitat will remain part of the landscape. More than two decades after the family first bought the property, its future has now been secured in a very different way: not through development, but by ensuring development cannot take place there.You use AI every day. articles.title: DR. MARC SIEGEL: What 18 years at Fox taught me about courage and faith
articles.summary: Benjamin Hall recalls the Ukraine war attack that killed his crew and the miraculous Ukrainian special forces rescue that he believes was a sign from God.
articles.body: I joined Fox in early 2008 as a contributor. I was struck from the beginning by the network's flexibility and creativity, allowing me to expand my role from expertise in infectious diseases to health policy and Obamacare. I was able to flex various journalistic muscles, too. I was sent to Phoenix to examine Sen. John McCain’s health records but ended up with the opportunity to deliver on-air reports. I began to report for the network in earnest in 2012, and then in the spring of 2013, during the Boston Marathon, when two self-radicalized brothers executed the largest terrorist attack on U.S. soil since 9/11, I managed to get permission from our top executives to head up there. DR MARC SIEGEL: TWENTY-FIVE YEARS AFTER 9/11, THE DEADLY HEALTH CRISIS IS STILL CLAIMING LIVES On the way, I somehow convinced the PR team at Massachusetts General Hospital (MGH) to grant me the very first interview with a survivor — a woman. Our excellent production team wasn’t expecting me, as we had our top reporters already in the field, but they quickly transitioned to supporting and guiding me. She had been blown off her feet and badly wounded her leg. Her would-be boyfriend had carried her down one-way streets (going in the opposite direction of the cars) to MGH. We were ready. She looked straight into the camera and said, "We can’t let the terrorists win. We must stay strong and not be afraid. Boston is a great city." Ten years later, another top Fox executive sent me to East Palestine, Ohio, following the train wreck there. One of the best field producers in the business came with me, and while I was in the neighborhood doughnut shop sampling the best doughnuts I’d ever had, she was assembling an array of guests who had all been injured or affected by the toxic smoke. FOX NEWS MEDIA'S SPOTLIGHT AWARDS CELEBRATE BEHIND-THE-SCENES STARS AS NETWORK NEARS 30 YEARS The ERs in the area were calling it "situational anxiety," but outside the temporary state health facility, I interviewed patients who were having trouble breathing while the smoke in the air gave everyone, myself included, a sore throat. People who swam in the river developed rashes, and the long-term health risks remained unknown. The angels of Fox are the executives, producers, and bookers who have the vision and work ethic to seek out and present stories that would otherwise be missed. We are a family that has developed strong bonds, and we look out for each other. When my father died earlier this year at age 102, the entire Fox management team, from the CEO on down, came to the funeral. The angels of Fox are the executives, producers, and bookers who have the vision and work ethic to seek out and present stories that would otherwise be missed. BENJAMIN HALL TACKLES GRUELING ONE WORLD TRADE CENTER CLIMB ON PROSTHETIC LEGS TO HONOR FALLEN HEROES Senior Correspondent Ben Hall brings out the best in the Fox team, and they inspire him. Chief National Security Correspondent Jennifer Griffin was crucial to arranging his extraction from Ukraine after a horrific near-death experience when his car was bombed and his cameraman and producer were killed in 2022. He survived, thanks to many angels, messengers from God, as I write in my new book, "THE ANGELS AMONG US." Here’s what Benjamin Hall shared with me about what he was thinking on the day he and his team were attacked in Ukraine: "At this moment of trying to stay strong, I think of how I am going to get home. I think of my children. Our car has burned totally to pieces, and we are down on the road, down a slight little dip in the road where we are lying, and this one car comes out of nowhere, and it drives past us. And I am shouting at it, ‘We’re here! We’re here!’ And it doesn’t see us, and it keeps driving. And it is a car of Ukrainian special forces, and this same car, amazingly, has engine trouble ten minutes or so down the road, and they have to stop to figure that out. And because of that, they drive back again!" Hall believes this event is a sign directly from God. DANA PERINO: THE UNTOLD STORY OF THE REMARKABLE PEOPLE WHO MAKE FOX NEWS POSSIBLE "I have pulled myself further up by this time, dragging myself along, up toward the road, and as the car comes back again, I don’t know it’s coming. There it is… The last thing I remember is this guy jumping out. He grabs my body armor, grabs the back of my arm, and pulls me along the ground, running to his car." Is the vision of his daughter that he sees after the missile hits actually an angel? It’s the question everyone has, and I ask it of Hall. MARTHA MACCALLUM: AFTER 22 YEARS, HERE'S WHY I'M GRATEFUL TO CALL FOX HOME "Yeah, 100%, either she is an angel that comes to me when I need her, and she gives me the strength I need, and she brings me back, or it is because my body and my mind are calling for her. It’s after the first and then the second shell, when I go into this other world, that’s when I get shrapnel in the eye, and it takes out part of my skull. So, I am already pretty badly injured at this point. Then the third shell takes off my leg, my foot. But I’ve no doubt that my daughter is sent to me, and either it is God who sends her or my body needs it, and my mind goes to the place it has to go to find the right strength." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Ben Hall’s father had recently died in 2022, and Hall had just buried him when he flew from his father’s funeral straight to Ukraine. Hall can feel his father is there with him as well. It’s as if his father’s life has joined with his own now that his spirit has moved on to the next world, into heaven. His father gives him strength. His daughter is there with him, and so is his father. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News loves Ben Hall, and his courage and strength inspire all of us. articles.title: US visa clash exposes Sudan’s forgotten war as foreign powers compete for strategic foothold
articles.summary: Abdel Fattah al-Burhan struck a defiant tone after Washington withheld his visa amid a dispute over a proposed 90-day humanitarian truce in Sudan.
articles.body: UNITED NATIONS — Sudan’s military leader is openly defying a U.S.-backed ceasefire push after Washington withheld his visa to attend the U.N. General Assembly, exposing a widening rift over a war that has become not only one of the world’s worst humanitarian disasters, but also a regional struggle for influence stretching to the Red Sea. Gen. Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, head of Sudan’s armed forces and de facto leader, had been expected in New York during UNGA before the Trump administration withheld his visa amid a dispute over a proposed 90-day humanitarian truce. Days later, Burhan struck a defiant tone from Khartoum. "We will keep our heads high. We will not accept bargaining, sell ourselves cheaply to anyone or bow to anyone," Burhan said Saturday, according to Anadolu Agency. "We do not need a visa to any country or anyone’s permission." WORLD LEADERS DESCEND ON NEW YORK FOR UNGA — BUT WHO REALLY HAS AMERICA’S EAR? The State Department has accused both Burhan’s Sudanese Armed Forces, or SAF, and the rival paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, of failing to make serious commitments to an immediate truce. "Neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces, nor their respective leaders, represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan," State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said Sept. 22, adding that the conduct of both leaders renders them "ineligible to govern the country." The State Department said both sides had instead intensified combat operations and drone strikes that killed civilians and said Washington had repeatedly asked them to accept a humanitarian truce "without preconditions" and commit to an inclusive political dialogue leading to civilian government. But a senior advisor to Burhan disputed Washington’s account in an on-camera interview with Fox News Digital on the sidelines of UNGA. SUDAN'S FORGOTTEN WAR LEAVES MILLIONS HUNGRY AS GLOBAL ATTENTION REMAINS ELSEWHERE Dr. Amjad Farid Al-Tayyib, the foreign affairs advisor to Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council, said Sudan never rejected the American ceasefire proposal and instead submitted technical comments on it. "We never rejected this proposal," Farid said. "The Sudanese government wants war with no one." Farid said a negotiating team had intended to accompany Burhan and accused Washington of undermining the very diplomatic process it was seeking to advance by preventing the delegation from traveling. The State Department declined to comment on Burhan’s specific visa case, citing its policy of not discussing individual visa decisions. A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital on background that Washington is instead focused on a broader diplomatic framework with Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the UAE through the Quad, linking a humanitarian truce and sustained aid access to a permanent ceasefire, civilian transition and reconstruction. "We are working with our partners to encourage the parties to agree to the humanitarian truce and guarantee humanitarian access, and to also ensure external military or financial support to the warring parties is cut off," the spokesperson said. The spokesperson added that the Quad supports the Quintet-led civilian political track and rejects parallel diplomatic processes that could fragment negotiations. The United Nations also challenged Washington over the visa decision. "We immediately raised with the U.S. authorities the issue regarding the denial of visa to the President of the Transitional Sovereign Council of the Sudan, who was scheduled to address the General Assembly this week," U.N. Secretary-General spokesman Stéphane Dujarric told Fox News Digital. PUTIN USING AFRICA AS ‘PURSE’ FOR UKRAINE WAR WHILE US FACES ‘INTELLIGENCE BLACK HOLE’: COMMANDER Cameron Hudson, a former director for African affairs on the National Security Council who also served as chief of staff to successive U.S. presidential special envoys for Sudan, said his understanding was that Washington had asked the Sudanese to send a delegation both to the U.N. and to Washington for talks on a ceasefire. He said the Sudanese were preparing to do so before Washington, in his understanding, made Burhan’s visa contingent on signing the ceasefire agreement before traveling. "It doesn’t fully make sense why the United States took this decision at the last minute," Hudson told Fox News Digital. Farid said the central dispute is whether the RSF would be required to withdraw from civilian areas it controls. He argued that freezing current lines of control risks turning a temporary ceasefire into a de facto partition of Sudan. The dispute comes against the backdrop of a brutal civil war that erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between Burhan and RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti. Both sides have been accused of serious violations, but Hudson told Fox News Digital that treating their records as interchangeable obscures an important distinction. "The RSF is committing war crimes on a scale and with an intention that the army does not," Hudson said. Hudson said SAF has struck civilian targets and committed war crimes, including through drone attacks, but said the RSF’s record goes significantly further. "They have committed mass rape, mass killing, torture, sexual enslavement," Hudson said, arguing that Western descriptions of "both sides" can create the impression that the two forces are committing the same crimes "on the same scale or with the same intention." U.N. investigators have also drawn distinctions while documenting abuses by both forces. AS WORLD FIXATES ON OTHER WARS, SUDAN SEES 12 MILLION FORCIBLY DISPLACED IN DEVASTATING CONFLICT A U.N. fact-finding mission reported in September 2025 that both SAF and RSF were responsible for direct, large-scale attacks against civilians and the destruction of critical civilian infrastructure. But it found that the RSF, particularly during its siege of El Fasher and surrounding areas, committed crimes against humanity including murder, torture, enslavement, rape, sexual slavery, forced displacement and persecution on ethnic, gender and political grounds. A separate U.N. Human Rights Office report released in February documented more than 6,000 killings during the first three days of the RSF’s final offensive on El Fasher and found that the violations could amount to war crimes and possible crimes against humanity. Farid nevertheless accused the U.N. and Western governments of creating what he called a ‘false equivalence’ between Sudan’s military and the RSF. "The U.N. is not staying neutral," he told Fox News Digital, arguing that international institutions have documented RSF atrocities without taking sufficient action against the group or those supporting it. Farid nevertheless accused the U.N. and Western governments of creating what he called a false equivalence between Sudan’s military and the RSF. U.N. Secretary-General spokesman Stéphane Dujarric rejected the allegation that the organization was equating the two sides. "This is not about equating two sides," Dujarric told Fox News Digital. "We focus on the facts, the violations that have been documented, and above all, the devastating toll this war has taken on civilians since 15 April 2023." Dujarric said both the RSF and SAF have used explosive weapons in densely populated areas and that the U.N. Human Rights Office has documented attacks affecting schools, hospitals, markets and religious sites. He pointed specifically to what he described as "particularly grave violations" by the RSF and affiliated forces in Darfur, including mass killings, sexual violence, torture, abductions and forced displacement, while noting that serious abuses have also been documented in SAF-controlled areas, including arbitrary detention, torture, ill-treatment and summary executions. The war, meanwhile, increasingly extends beyond Sudan’s borders. Foreign backing has become a central feature of the conflict. A July 2026 UK government assessment, drawing on U.N. and other reporting, said the RSF had benefited from support networks involving the UAE and neighboring countries, while SAF had received backing from states including Egypt, Iran, Pakistan and Turkey. The UAE has repeatedly denied providing military support to the RSF. Fox News Digital reached out to the UAE Embassy in Washington and the UAE mission to the U.N. but did not receive a response in time for publication. BAB EL-MANDEB STRAIT FACES GROWING THREAT AS HOUTHI ATTACKS RAISE FEARS OF A SECOND HORMUZ Hudson said the RSF’s foreign relationships are only part of a much larger regional competition. He said Egypt, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Qatar have supported the army to varying degrees, while outside powers pursue their own strategic interests in Sudan. That competition increasingly centers on Sudan’s Red Sea coastline. "There is a regional battle of influence among neighboring states and regional states who want to be able to control Sudan’s Red Sea coastline," Hudson said, pointing to potential military, port and economic access. "Superimposed on top of the conflict inside Sudan is a regional proxy conflict for influence in Sudan and in the wider Horn of Africa, Red Sea region," he said. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also said foreign powers are central to prolonging the war. "What’s happening in Sudan would not be happening were it not for external actors supporting one side or the other," Rubio told reporters during UNGA week, describing U.S. efforts to secure even limited humanitarian agreements as "very frustrating." Rubio said the parties have repeatedly agreed to commitments only to abandon them when one side believes it is gaining the upper hand. "There are external actors. I’m not going to single them out. You know who they are," Rubio said. articles.title: Christa Pike execution: Tennessee governor rejects plea for clemency
articles.summary: If the execution proceeds, Pike would be the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
articles.body:
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has denied a clemency request from death row inmate Christa Pike, who is scheduled to be executed by lethal injection on Wednesday.

Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

She may have one last chance at halting her execution as her attorneys have filed a petition with the US Supreme Court hoping for a last-minute reprieve.

If it proceeds, Pike would be the first woman to be executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.

Killer Christa Pike to be executed within days - but her defence say she's a victim too

"After deliberate consideration of Christa Gail Pike's request for clemency, and after a thorough review of the case, I am upholding the sentence of the State of Tennessee and do not plan to intervene," Governor Lee said in a statement.

Pike's legal team had filed the clemency petition earlier this month, requesting that her death sentence be commuted to life in prison.

Moving ahead with Pike's execution puts Tennessee "on singular footing", her attorneys said, as she would be the first person the state "executes in the modern death penalty era who was a teenager at the time of the offence".

Attorneys Stephen Ferrell, Kelly Gleason and Randy Spivey said the governor's decision "leaves unanswered vital questions about Tennessee's execution protocol".

"With this decision, the State of Tennessee is ignoring what both science and our legal system have decided: an 18-year-old brain is not an adult brain, and 18 is too young to face execution," they said in a statement on Monday.

The murder of Colleen Slemmer created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when the 19-year-old was found with a pentagram - a symbol of Satanic ritual - carved into her chest.

Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.

A year later, she was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to death, while then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp- who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

At the time of her incarceration, the 21-year-old was the youngest person on death row, according to the Tennessee Department of Corrections.

Pike is scheduled to be executed on 30 September after years of failed appeals.

Colleen's mother has insisted she wants Pike's execution to move forward so that her daughter "finally can be resting".

Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse , abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.

"The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists," her attorneys said. "Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women."

In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider.

articles.title: Explain legal basis of MDR, Supreme Court tells Centre
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Monday asked the Centre, RBI and National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) to explain under which provision of law the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Monday asked the Centre, RBI and National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) to explain under which provision of law the merchant discount rate (MDR) on UPI transactions was imposed, even though it refused to stay its implementation from Oct 15."Is it a tax or a fee? If it is not a tax or a fee, then what is the executive scope of making this expropriation on transactions? What is the character of this expropriation?" asked a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana while hearing a PIL that argued that MDR charges on UPI transactions would make people revert to cash dealings, which would encourage accumulation of black money.Additional solicitor general N Venkataraman (ASG) said MDR is not a tax or a fee, nor an expropriation as govt will not get even a paisa from it. It is akin to service charges levied by banks on transactions done earlier through credit and debit cards, though MDR's scope is much more restricted. He said that 96% of the transactions are exempted from MDR, while from within the balance 4%, essential services will attract a flat charge of Rs 5. For the rest, transactions above Rs 75,000 will attract a maximum MDR of Rs 300. Justice Bagchi asked, "What is this service charge? Please file an affidavit and explain. It cannot be through executive fiat."Explaining the operation of credit and debit cards, the predecessors of the UPI mode of transferring money, and the service charge attached to such transactions because of the involvement of banks and the aggregator, Venkatraman said there is no difference between UPI and the previous system, and it involves a service charge payable to banks and aggregator NPCI, which facilitates the transactions. "Govt does not take a rupee from it," he said.Justice Bagchi said, "When it is a charge in terms of provisions of the Income Tax Act, on whose hand is it an income?" Venkatraman said the provision of the Income Tax Act cited by the court is an enabling provision which recognises UPI money transfers as a valid transaction, nothing more, nothing less.When the bench asked who takes the MDR amount, the Centre said it will be the banks and the aggregator, like for credit or debit cards. It has nothing to do with law as it is purely an administrative mechanism, the ASG said.CJI Kant said, "It appears more technical than law. It would be better if the govt, RBI and NPCI file their affidavits explaining the entire issue." Referring to full-page advertisements in Monday newspapers explaining the MDR, the CJI said, "We have read your advance arguments in the newspapers. Yet, you file a detailed affidavit." The petitioner's counsel sought a stay on the imposition of MDR, a plea Venkatraman opposed, saying it will come into force on Oct 15. The bench brushed aside the plea for a stay and asked the Centre, RBI and NPCI to file affidavits in four weeks.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Unis are offering degrees in content creation for £30,000. But are they worth it?
articles.summary: Content creation degrees aim to help people make money from their social media posts.
articles.body:
As university courses go it may raise a few eyebrows, but Destiny McGowan has no doubt that hers was very useful.

In July the 21-year-old graduated from Nottingham Trent University with a degree in content creation.

As well as teaching how to best make videos and posts for Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, the course also focused on how to build audiences, engage with brands and monetise your content.

"I always wanted to be an entrepreneur, so for me the course was about the transferable skills that I believed I would gain," says Destiny, pointing to both the social media and business aspects she was taught.

It's early on in her career, and Destiny refuses to disclose precisely what she is earning, but says she's already making money.

In addition to posting about fashion on her own accounts, she makes videos for others, and has also been hired as a TikTok live selling host, presenting products for sale on camera.

She says the course gave her access to equipment, technology and industry contacts.

"The incredible people I've met through panels that the university hosted would take someone five to 10 years to get to that place," she explains.

Nottingham Trent says its content creation degree, which it launched in 2022, provides "hands-on experience".

Several universities in the UK now offer such courses. The University of Brighton says it teaches students how to create "content that cuts through the noise".

Meanwhile in the US, Arizona State University say its similar qualification allows students to "turn your creativity into content that connects with audiences".

Yet you'd be paying a lot of money for this. The three-year degrees at Nottingham Trent and Brighton both currently cost £9,790 per year for UK students, while the standard annual fee at Arizona State is $14,724 (£11,000) for a resident of that state.

More than £2m spent by government on influencers since July 2024

Knightenator, a UK-based, full-time content creator, isn't sure. "I don't think I would have taken the course," she says.

The 31-year-old, who doesn't reveal her real name, has been posting videos about gaming and travel on social media since 2015. She now has 65,000 followers on Twitch, and more than 100,000 on TikTok.

It is her full-time job, and while she won't reveal how much money she makes, she says she gets most of her income from deals with brands that she promotes.

"Honestly, from my experience, I don't think companies would care too much if you had a content creator degree," she says.

She adds that the internet is saturated with free advice on how to get started. "If you have the drive to want to become a content creator, the tips are out there, and you don't need to commit to a three-year degree."

Her advice is to watch other people's content and find your own niche. "I honestly think that you don't need much in this day and age at this moment to be able to do it."

But fellow content creator Aiesha Beasley from Phoenix, Arizona disagrees.

The 36-year-old, who posts about food, fashion and lifestyle, says she would have enrolled on one of these courses if they had been available when she first started blogging on Tumblr in the early 2010s.

She believes a degree would have given her a "clearer pathway", particularly when it comes to how to earn a living.

"You really do have to have a business mindset on: how can I transition this from a hobby into something that makes me money?" says Aiesha.

She adds that such courses are "ahead of the curve" in recognising that content creation is increasingly an important part of marketing.

"Now you have to have a digital presence," she explains, "whether you are a business owner or an entrepreneur or building a personal brand."

The degrees by the likes of Nottingham Trent and Arizona State come as the content creator economy booms on both sides of the Atlantic. YouTube content creators alone contribute £2.2bn to the UK economy, according to one report last year.

Meanwhile, one in three people aged between 18 and 30 in the US wish to become an influencer, a 2024 survey suggests.

However, Jacky Gurr, course leader and senior lecturer for content creation at Nottingham Trent University, points out that the majority of people on the course are not actually aspiring to become influencers.

For Gurr, content creation is a professional skill that organisations increasingly need, whether someone runs their own business, works in-house, joins an agency or works freelance across multiple clients.

"Those skills absolutely can be taught. Students learn how to plan and produce video content, develop campaigns, understand audiences, analyse performance data and adapt strategies based on that data."

She adds that the business side of content creation "is an important part of the degree", where they discuss monetisation and the commercial side of the industry.

But for anyone who thinks a university degree will lead to overnight success as an influencer, Jacky Gurr has these words of caution: "So much of being a successful influencer is about luck, and we can't teach luck or personality."

articles.title: Three Egyptian security officials convicted of kidnapping Italian student Giulio Regeni
articles.summary: Giulio Regeni's tortured body was found days after he went missing on a research trip to Egypt in 2016, while studying at Cambridge University.
articles.body:
Three Egyptian security officials have been convicted by a Rome court over the kidnapping of an Italian student whose tortured body was found in Cairo a decade ago.

The men, who were tried in absentia, denied the charges. On Monday they were sentenced to 10 years in prison on charges of aggravated kidnapping. A fourth Egyptian defendant was acquitted.

Giulio Regeni, 28, was studying for a doctorate at Cambridge University when he went missing while on a research trip in Egypt in 2016.

Days later, his mutilated body was found in a ditch near Cairo. An autopsy later revealed he had been tortured.

Italian and Egyptian prosecutors originally investigated the case together, but reached opposing conclusions.

Egyptian authorities argued criminal gangsters were to blame for Regeni's murder and suggested various other explanations for his death, including a car accident, failed drug deal, or botched robbery.

They also denied any state involvement in Regeni's disappearance or death.

But prosecutors in Rome concluded that the Egyptian national security agency was involved in the crime.

The four defendants were Gen Tariq Sabir, Col Usham Helmi, Col Athar Kamel Mohamed Ibrahim and Maj Magdi Ibrahim Abdelal Sharif. Sabir was acquitted.

Rome's chief prosecutor and a lawyer for Regeni's family welcomed the verdict.

"From today, people around the world can feel safer," Alessandra Ballerini, the family's lawyer, said. "Impunity can be defeated and democracies can place limits on arbitrary power."

Regeni's family have campaigned throughout the decade for justice. As the verdict was read out, there was silence from family members and supporters in court who wore yellow t-shirts and badges, the colour of their campaign, AFP reported.

Regeni was abducted on 25 January 2016 while carrying out research for his PhD at Cambridge University on Egypt's independent trade unions - a politically controversial topic in Egypt.

His mother told the Italian parliament in 2018 that her son's body was so disfigured that she was only able to identify him by the tip of his nose. Prosecutors said he sustained injuries that showed he was beaten with "kicks, fists, sticks and clubs", and that he died from a broken neck.

The verdict was the end of a years-long effort by Italy to prosecute the security officials.

The trial, initially scheduled for 2021, was suspended due to concerns prosecutors had been unable to track down the defendants to issue the charges.

However, in September 2023, Italy's Constitutional Court allowed the trial to go ahead.

While extradition remains unlikely, the convictions could renew diplomatic tensions between Italy and Egypt.

articles.title: Australian students went scuba diving to rebuild an oyster reef; 28 underwater structures quickly attracted oysters and marine life
articles.summary: Australian high school students have taken part in an underwater experiment aimed at bringing native oyster reefs back to Coffin Bay in South Australia.
articles.body: Australian high school students have taken part in an underwater experiment aimed at bringing native oyster reefs back to Coffin Bay in South Australia. After receiving SCUBA training, the students helped place 28 restoration units across different sites in the bay. The structures were made from old oyster shells inside mesh crates, creating a base where young oysters and other marine organisms could settle. When researchers returned three months later, every unit had attracted oysters, while hundreds of other marine organisms had also colonised the structures, according to a 2026 study published in People and Nature.Australian students learned scuba diving to rebuild the oyster reefThe project brought local teenagers directly into marine restoration rather than keeping the research work on land. The study involved 10 students aged about 15 to 17 from 2 regional high schools, who worked with diving professionals to prepare and deploy the experiment.Before entering the water, the students completed SCUBA training and received PADI Open Water Diver certification. The training was provided without cost to their families through funding from an Environmental Citizen Science Small Grant from the South Australian Government.The students also helped collect old oyster shells from historical reef locations. These shells had been buried beneath sediment and were carefully excavated by hand while diving. After organisms were removed, the shells were cleaned, dried and sterilised before being used in the experiment.Why were oysters being restored in Coffin BayCoffin Bay once had some of South Australia's largest native oyster reefs. The study explains that the native oyster Ostrea angasi was historically an important part of the seafloor, and the first colonial settlement in the area was even called Oyster Town because of the productive oyster dredge fishery.That fishery did not last. Decades of overharvesting drove native oysters to functional extinction in the area, while dredging also removed the shells that young oysters need to settle and build new reefs. Sediment runoff later covered much of the remaining shell material, leaving little natural recovery after dredging ended.The bay still has an oyster industry based on introduced Pacific oysters, but the researchers were interested in whether native oysters could once again establish themselves using suitable habitat.What did the 28 underwater structures containThe researchers placed 28 restoration units across 8 sites in Coffin Bay. Four of the locations were inside no-fishing Sanctuary Zones, while four nearby sites were used as control areas.Each unit contained 100 clean native oyster shells inside a plastic mesh crate measuring 40 by 20 by 15 centimetres. The open structure allowed water and small animals to move through the shells while providing a hard surface for young oysters to settle.Two concrete settlement panels were also attached to each unit. The experiment was deployed during the oyster recruitment season, from January to April, and all 28 units went into the water on the same day.Three months later, the students returned with researchers to retrieve the structures. The team examined the oysters and other organisms found inside them, with smaller creatures later identified in the laboratory.Analysing the underwater structures after 3 monthsThe underwater units quickly became occupied. Oysters recruited to every restoration unit, although the number varied substantially between locations.Across the sites, individual units contained between 26 to 2,388 oysters. Dutton Bay recorded the highest average recruitment, with about 1,257 oysters per unit, compared with 348 at Kellidie Bay and 160 at Yangie Bay.The settlement panels also recorded large numbers of young oysters, ranging from 44 to 20,065 oysters per square metre. The researchers found that recruitment differed between locations, showing that some parts of Coffin Bay may provide more favourable conditions for rebuilding reefs than others.The structures were not used only by oysters. After three months, 3,342 organisms representing 68 faunal species had colonised the restoration units. The researchers also recorded new occurrence and distribution information for several species in the region, including two fish species.The study found that marine life differed between locations and between Sanctuary and control areas. Sanctuary areas also showed higher measures of species diversity, although the effects varied depending on the site.What did the students hope to gain from the projectThe underwater work was not simply a science exercise for the teenagers. Researchers examined why the students wanted to participate by analysing their application essays.They identified 23 different motivations, which appeared 297 times across the 10 essays. Personal benefits accounted for 36% of the motivations, while environmental benefits and community or social opportunities each accounted for 32%.Students described gaining experience, learning about marine science, developing possible career skills and spending time in the ocean. Environmental reasons included protecting local biodiversity and helping nature. Others were motivated by their connection to Coffin Bay and the chance to contribute to their own community.Half of the students specifically recognised the project as a potential career-building experience, including opportunities connected with conservation and environmental work.Importance of this oyster experiment for future restorationFor the researchers, the experiment provided two kinds of information at once. It showed that native oysters could still recruit in large numbers in Coffin Bay, while also giving local students and residents direct experience with restoration.The findings suggested that restoring the lost reefs could be feasible using natural oyster recruitment. Recruitment varied between sites, but oysters appeared on every restoration unit, including areas where the historical reef ecosystem had been heavily degraded.The researchers said the knowledge generated by the project subsequently enabled the first oyster reef restoration on South Australia's Eyre Peninsula, with the work continuing through community participation.You use AI every day. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Monday refused to accept the timeline proposed by FSSAI for the implementation of front-of-pack labelling (FoPL) for food products, including four months' time for framing regulations and a 365-day voluntary implementation period for food businesses after notification, saying it was unreasonable and decided to fix the timeline for the food regulator.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran, however, made it clear to the regulator that it has to implement the court's order, which is in the national interest, in true spirit and not delay implementation. It asked why the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) had fixed such a long timeframe to implement it as consultations with stakeholders had taken place in 2022."Why voluntary compliance for a year?... Why do you want to start afresh with the exercise of hearing and calling for objections? You started in 2022, what did you do in the last four years?"SC also termed advocate Rajiv Shankar Dvivedi's plea for immediate implementation of FoPL as unreasonable and said it would pass an order to fix all contentious issues.Additional solicitor general Brijender Chahar, appearing for FSSAI, said the process initiated in 2022 was relating to a star-rating system based on an entirely different criterion. The bench, however, said the issue involved was very important and there should not be any more delay."We appreciate your initiative but there is a lot which is required to be done to give meaningful effect to what we want to achieve," SC said.Reserving the order, SC told FSSAI, "Whatever order we now pass will be binding on you, and we expect you to implement it scrupulously. We are undertaking this entire exercise for the good of the nation and for the good of citizens. We will now pronounce the final order. And we will keep it after some time to report due compliance in each and every direction. Do not disappoint us on the day when the matter comes up for reporting compliance."Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: DA defends decision not to prosecute alleged Cornell 'gang rape' case in 2024
articles.summary: Tompkins County DA Matthew Van Houten announced he was reopening the case.
articles.body:
Prosecutors in upstate New York are defending their decision not to bring charges in 2024 after an alleged "gang rape" at a Cornell University fraternity.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten described the allegations as "morally disturbing" but argued that the facts he knew at the time did not support a prosecution.

"If what was said on social media about this case was true, those fraternity members would be in prison right now," Van Houten told ABC News.

Van Houten argued that Jane Doe's account of the incident from 2024 suggested that she consented to the sexual activity. He said that she did not withdraw her consent, and that when she raised concerns, the fraternity members "stopped and did not pursue what they were doing."

"She clearly consented in the beginning, and there was never any indication that she changed that to the things that she participated in," he said. "There is a disconnect in the sense of how the community and how social media has understood this to have happened. If at any point Jane Doe had said, 'I don't consent to this anymore,' or in those words, or in any form of communication. If there had been continued sexual activity, contact by these individuals, that would be a crime. But that's not what was alleged in her statement."

Van Houten acknowledged that his office did not examine a photo of the fraternity's Snapchat group, but he argued that the messages do not change his view of the case.

He called the messages, "disgusting and vulgar and immoral."

"But the question that we analyzed was: Did Jane Doe consent to what happened, and was she unable to consent?" he said. "I'm not clear on exactly how that was given to us, or if anyone here looked at it. That was not critical to our analysis, as I mentioned earlier. The issue was her consent, and if you take that Snapchat being vile and crude and vulgar, that did not have any relevance to the issue of whether Jane Doe consented to what was happening," Van Houten said.

The DA's comments come a day after his office announced it would be reopening the 2024 case in light of Jane Doe's civil lawsuit alleging that she was drugged, assaulted and gang raped by seven former and current members of the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell.

Cornell's Chi Phi chapter was barred from campus after the alleged Oct. 19, 2024, incident, though none of the individuals allegedly involved faced criminal charges, according to the DA.

An attorney for Jane Doe responded to Van Houten's written statement on Monday, alleging his client's claims were not investigated thoroughly.

"It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she was never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint," Thomas P. Giuffra said.

Giuffra also raised concerns that prosecutors might have lost critical evidence because of the two-year delay in investigating the case.

"I believe that opportunities to fully investigate these crimes were lost. We will never fully know what occurred or the identities of everyone who was involved that night," he said.

Van Houten said his office plans to meet with Jane Doe to "establish a rapport" before having her testify before the grand jury this fall. He added that he requested some of the documents from Cornell's Title IX investigation (through Jane Doe) and suggested that some of the fraternity members might testify.

Van Houten argued his office is constrained by New York's laws on sexual assault and consent, which present a high bar to a potential prosecution.

"The law in New York State is clear that if you are voluntarily intoxicated or under the influence of drugs – such that your judgment is impaired — that does not legally, under the penal law, constitute your inability to consent," Van Houten said. "That's a very difficult concept, but it's a concept that I am constrained by when I apply the law to the case."

The university said in a new statement on Monday that it "supports the decision of the Tompkins County District Attorney (DA) to provide an opportunity for the victim's story, in the 2024 Chi Phi fraternity Sexual Assault case, to be heard by a criminal grand jury."

"Cornell also conducted a thorough Title IX investigation, which is separate from a criminal proceeding, over the course of several months," Monday's statement said. "During that investigation temporary suspensions and other restrictive measures were used. After investigation, and pursuant to federal law, the matter was sent to a hearing where a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days. The complainant and respondents had the opportunity to testify and present evidence. At its conclusion, the hearing panel issued a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell. None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement."

Jane Doe's lawyers allege that the fraternity members "were afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell."

The fraternity was closed in 2024, the school said.

"Any suggestion that the University did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," Cornell said on Monday. "A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault."

ABC News has reached out to Chi Phi for a comment.

An attorney for one of the defendants denied the allegations and said the incident detailed in the complaint "did not happen."

"We look forward to confronting the plaintiff in a court of law for her selfishly false claims with both the evidence and her own words." Attorney Jeremy Saland said.

Another defendant also denied engaging in sexual activity or drug use, though he acknowledged that he sent a message that was included in the complaint.

articles.title: Could psychedelic therapy become NHS treatment for mental health?
articles.summary: Could hallucinogenic drugs become part of mainstream NHS care to treat depression?
articles.body:
From retreats in the Amazon to clinical trials in Newcastle, psychedelic therapy is attracting growing attention as a possible treatment for depression. Could hallucinogenic drugs one day become part of mainstream NHS care?

Claire Torpey had tried traditional forms of mental health support, including counselling. But she says there was still something she could not shake.

"There was a deep sadness. I was living in chronic anxiety," she says.

Claire, from Tynemouth, North Tyneside, spent part of her childhood in care and says the challenges she faced growing up were compounded by the deaths of her father and grandmother in consecutive years.

"There wasn't anything that was really moving the needle from my internal state. I was deeply sad and I didn't want to be here."

Seeking alternatives, Claire travelled to South and Central America to attend retreats where participants legally take psychedelics as part of guided therapeutic programmes.

The retreats involved psilocybin, the psychoactive compound found in magic mushrooms, and ayahuasca, a traditional Amazonian brew containing the psychedelic compound DMT.

Psychedelic tourism has grown in popularity, but experts warn that unethical and unregulated practices can pose serious risks. There have been reports of participants dying after attending retreats and ceremonies abroad.

For Claire, however, she says the experience was transformative.

"It wasn't until I started taking these medicines that it started to lift," she says.

"I started to find a place of peace and happiness. It took me on a journey of forgiveness.

"I don't believe that normal talk therapies would have got me there."

In the UK, psilocybin and DMT are Class A drugs and are classified as Schedule 1 substances, meaning they are considered to have no recognised medicinal use.

Yet interest in psychedelic-assisted therapy is growing.

At Newcastle's Care Pathway Enhancement (CaPE) Clinic, run by Cumbria, Northumberland, Tyne and Wear NHS Foundation Trust, researchers are investigating whether psilocybin could help treat conditions including depression.

The theory is that, when used in a controlled setting, psychedelics can help people process difficult thoughts and emotions. Some researchers liken the mind to a snow globe: the drugs temporarily disrupt established thought patterns, allowing thoughts and feelings to settle differently and providing new perspectives on past experiences.

Consultant psychiatrist Dr Mourad Wahba, who leads the research, says participants often report significant shifts in how they view themselves and their experiences.

"The idea is that through having this experience, people can change their behaviours and patterns of thinking," he says.

The treatment involves extensive preparation and support before and after dosing sessions.

Clinical psychologist Tom Sharp helps facilitate the trials. Participants receive psilocybin in capsule form before spending up to eight hours in a specially designed dosing room under the supervision of therapists.

"People can develop a sense of what might have caused their depression," he says.

Researchers are keen to temper expectations.

"This type of work isn't some silver bullet," says Sharp. "It doesn't turn off depression."

Wahba agrees. While early findings are encouraging, he says larger studies are still needed to establish how effective the treatments are and whether any benefits can be sustained in the longer term.

The Royal College of Psychiatrists has backed further research into psychedelic-assisted therapy.

Dr David Cousins, chair of its psychopharmacology committee, said: "The College supports further research into psychedelics such as psilocybin, which have the potential to help in the treatment of people with conditions such as depression, including those who are less responsive to other forms of care."

Some researchers believe psychedelic-assisted therapy may offer longer-lasting benefits for certain patients by helping them address underlying thoughts, emotions and behaviours rather than simply managing symptoms.

However, Cousins cautioned against seeking treatment outside regulated settings.

"We strongly advise against people self-medicating or seeking access to unregulated treatments as there are risks in doing so."

Supporters stress that psychedelic therapy is very different from recreational drug use. In clinical settings, participants are screened, monitored and supported before, during and after treatment.

Some UK charities and organisations are also helping people access psychedelic therapy overseas.

Keith John Abraham, founder of Heroic Hearts Project UK, helps former military personnel attend retreats involving ayahuasca to support conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder.

"Most people come out of this and feel like they've got a renewed sense of energy and purpose," he says.

Abraham, an army veteran, turned to psychedelic therapy after struggling with the effects of military service.

"Afghanistan came at a great personal cost to me.

"I went down the traditional avenues and I found they didn't work for me and became quite desperate."

Abraham says psychedelic therapy helped him make significant progress, but warns against portraying it as a miracle cure.

"We shouldn't come into this assuming that all of our problems will be resolved. But life can be very much improved."

Abraham describes psychedelic therapy as the "future of mental health care".

Robin Daly, founder of the cancer charity Yes to Life, believes psychedelic-assisted therapy could also help some people cope with the emotional impact of serious illness.

He says a cancer diagnosis can leave people confronting questions about mortality, purpose and the future, and that psilocybin may help some patients come to terms with that reality.

"It's not about going off into la-la land," he says.

"It's about being able to accommodate the fact, 'OK, I'm in this situation, I have cancer', but to put it in a much bigger context."

While stressing that psilocybin is not a cure for cancer, he describes its potential impact on some patients as "revolutionary".

He believes access should not be limited to people who can afford to travel overseas for treatment.

Researchers argue progress is being slowed by regulation.

Wahba says obtaining licences to work with Schedule 1 substances can significantly delay studies.

"Let's say I start talking about a study in June. We apply for the licence in June or July. We might not get the licence until January," he says.

"So far, the risks aren't as pronounced as we would see with a lot of other medications. It just seems quite prohibitive at this point."

Looking ahead, he hopes psychedelic-assisted therapy could one day sit alongside existing NHS treatments.

"Giving patients choice is number one. So, it being part of our menu would be the ideal scenario for me."

The Home Office says it is considering advice on reducing barriers to research involving controlled drugs while ensuring safeguards remain in place.

The UK's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency says it facilitates clinical research, but it is still too early to know whether psychedelic treatments might one day become routinely available.

articles.title: Government mulls steps to save rabi crops from drought
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Apprehending the possibility of deficient rainfall in the upcoming sowing season, Centre Monday discussed contingency measures to minimise its
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Apprehending the possibility of deficient rainfall in the upcoming sowing season, Centre Monday discussed contingency measures to minimise its impact on rabi (winter-sown) crops, with Union agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan calling for data-driven planning, stronger Centre-state coordination, weekly crop monitoring, balanced fertiliser use and water budgeting.Amid indications that the kharif (summer-sown) crops' output may not match last year's level despite progress in acreage, the minister, while addressing farm scientists and policymakers at a national conference, also emphasised the need to drive the rabi strategy through less water-consuming pulses and oilseeds.The conference was convened to discuss the farm strategy, keeping in view the current drought situation in many states so that low moisture content in the soil and shortage of water for irrigation due to deficient rainfall do not impact farming significantly. The sowing of rabi crops such as wheat and mustard begins in Oct.Centre will send teams to Karnataka and Maharashtra to assess the drought situation. Nearly two-thirds of Maharashtra has been affected, and the state has already declared a drought, while Karnataka is also facing drought-like conditions due to a monsoon rainfall deficit of 30%.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Delhi Police file non-cognisable report against minister Parvesh Verma after complaint over slap
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has filed a non-cognisable report (NCR) in connection with a complaint by Sahib Singh, who was slapped by PWD minister Parvesh
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi Police has filed a non-cognisable report (NCR) in connection with a complaint by Sahib Singh, who was slapped by PWD minister Parvesh Verma. Police also said an FIR under sections related to extortion was registered on the complaint of an assistant engineer of the PWD against unknown person(s).AAP national convener Arvind Kejriwal, meanwhile, visited the road stretch in Tilak Nagar and demanded that Verma be dismissed and arrested. “The road surface can just be pulled apart by hand. Never before in Delhi has such a shoddy road been built,” he said.Yesterday, when a video was being made about this very corruption, minister Pravesh Verma slapped a boy in a fit of rage… We used to hear that roads like these were built in remote villages and far-flung areas of the country. Delhi is the national capital. We also ran the govt in Delhi for 10 years, but roads of this kind were never built during our tenure... Clearly, there has been a lot of corruption and it should be investigated,” Kejriwal said. He also interacted with local residents and heard their concerns.“Action under relevant sections of law has been taken on the complaints of Sahib Singh and the assistant engineer, PWD. Some other complaints have also been received on the incident, which will be taken up during the course of probe,” police said. Police sources said Singh said in his complaint that he was slapped, an allegation that falls under a non-cognisable offence. It was done under Section 115 (voluntarily causing hurt) of BNS.Meanwhile, the PWD engineer alleged that he was being extorted in connection with road construction work, following which a case was registered against unknown person(s) at Tilak Nagar police station. A non-cognisable case is one in which police cannot arrest an accused without a warrant. Such offences are generally considered less serious than cognisable offences. Police cannot investigate a non-cognisable offence without an order from a magistrate. Police are also not authorised to register an FIR for such an offence without obtaining the magistrate’s permission.Earlier in the day, Kejriwal posted a video message on X, addressing the PM. “PM Modi gets up at midnight, makes reels... and says, ‘I will build a rapport with Gen-Z.’ You will slap Gen-Z and then say that you will build a relationship with Gen-Z. That is why Gen-Z is so angry with you... articles.title: Lost songs from Divinyls frontwoman Chrissy Amphlett found in garage
articles.summary: Divinyls frontwoman Chrissy Amphlett recorded the songs with Split Enz's Tim Finn in 1998.
articles.body:
More than a decade after her death, the voice of Australian rock icon Chrissy Amphlett will be heard like never before after three lost songs were discovered in a garage.

The trailblazing frontwoman of rock band Divinyls, Amphlett's trademark husky voice and charismatic stage presence brought the world the 1990 number one track I Touch Myself as well as earlier hits Pleasure and Pain (1985) and Boys in Town (1981).

Years before her 2013 death, Amphlett recorded three songs with Tim Finn, former lead singer of New Zealand's Split Enz, in 1998. The tracks were thought to be lost until Finn found them in his garage in 2023.

On Friday, the songs will be released in an EP titled Some Times.

In an interview with Australian Story, a documentary programme by national broadcaster ABC, Finn recalled the 1998 recording session with Amphlett in Sydney.

"It was a good time for us to meet because she was looking for something new, something different in her life musically," Finn said.

Around that time, Amphlett had split with fellow band member, guitarist Mark McEntee after a tumultuous relationship and was growing close to drummer Charley Drayton, according to the documentary. The pair would later marry.

Over several days, he and Amphlett wrote a trio of songs and headed into the studio to record them, with Drayton on the drums.

"She was so focused," Finn said. "She just wanted to get it right... I was in the presence of great talent, great charisma."

In a social media post on Monday about the 1998 session, Finn said he had reached out to Amphlett having been a great admirer of her work.

"We hadn't met previously but instantly felt a bond, a camaraderie of shared history as ex-lead singers of two brilliant bands," Finn wrote on Monday.

When the session wrapped up, Finn took the recordings home and planned to work on it, but "they were never fully realised".

In 2023, Drayton contacted Finn, about the 1998 recordings.

"I thought they were lost to the universe but remarkably found the two-inch tape in my garage," Finn wrote in the post, describing the songs as "incredibly important to me, Charley and those close to Chrissy".

"It was still in perfect condition and we are now able to share these songs with you."

articles.title: US military to guard midterms after Donald Trump gutted agency that protects elections
articles.summary: US military intelligence and cybersecurity agencies will help protect American election systems during the November midterm elections, defence secretary
articles.body: US military intelligence and cybersecurity agencies will help protect American election systems during the November midterm elections, defence secretary Pete Hegseth has said.The National Security Agency and other military cyber units have long assisted with monitoring election infrastructure and defending it against possible hacking attempts. Election systems were designated as “critical infrastructure” in 2017, paving the way for greater federal cybersecurity support.Hegseth's announcement comes weeks before Election Day on November 3, with early voting already underway.Military steps in as civilian capacity shrinksThe announcement follows major changes to the civilian agency responsible for protecting US election infrastructure.President Donald Trump has significantly reduced the role of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, or CISA, within the Department of Homeland Security. The agency was specifically created to help protect critical infrastructure, including election systems.CISA last week released an election infrastructure security plan outlining possible threats to voting systems and the assistance it could provide to state and local election officials.David Becker, a former US Justice Department attorney who now heads the nonprofit Center for Election Innovation & Research, questioned the timing of the latest move.“If the administration was serious about assisting state and local election officials, they shouldn't have dismantled all of the federal government's election cybersecurity capacity and fired all their experts in early 2025,” he said.Becker said the short timeframe before the election “suggests this is just theater”.Concerns over possible interferenceCybersecurity assistance from the NSA and US Cyber Command is not new. However, election experts, civil rights groups and Democratic officials have expressed concern about possible government interference in voting and ballot-counting processes.Trump has continued to make unsubstantiated claims about widespread election fraud and has sought changes to established election procedures.The Supreme Court recently blocked an attempt by Trump to restrict mail voting. It has, however, allowed the use of a federal database to verify the citizenship of voters.What Hegseth orderedIn a September 22 memo made public on Monday, Hegseth instructed defence intelligence officials to use all available resources to protect election systems from foreign threats.“to defend our election infrastructure from foreign malign influence and ensure that every lawful voter can cast their ballot free from foreign intimidation, coercion, or fear.”The move places military cyber capabilities alongside existing state, local and federal efforts to protect voting infrastructure ahead of the November elections.You use AI every day.
